title: Why AI’s trillion-dollar buildout depends on the fiber path between data centers
summary: Data center spending is set to pass $1 trillion this year, and most of the attention stays on GPUs and power inside the building. As AI clusters spread across sites, planning the optical links between buildings is becoming just as important.
body_markdown:
[Dell’Oro Group projects](https://www.delloro.com/newsroom/ai-infrastructure-buildouts-and-memory-cost-inflation-drove-data-center-capex-higher-in-1q-2026/) worldwide data center capital spending will pass $1 trillion by the end of 2026.[Cignal AI forecasts](https://cignal.ai/2025/07/800g-coherent-pluggable-shipments-to-exceed-1b-revenue-in-2026/) that sales of 800ZR and 800ZR+ coherent pluggables will surpass $1 billion in revenue this year. Most of the focus is on what happens inside the building: accelerators, power and cooling. The fiber path between buildings is getting less attention than it deserves.


AI no longer fits in a single building because one site can only draw so much power. As AI training outgrows a single facility, operators spread the work across several data centers in a metro area or region. This approach, often called scale-across, only works if the links between sites behave like an extension of the data center fabric: high capacity, predictable latency and simple to grow.


**Why scale-across puts pressure on the optical layer**


Data center interconnect (DCI) has largely been associated with moving storage replicas, backups and cloud traffic between sites. AI training traffic, however, is different. Synchronizing model training across sites generates much larger, sustained flows that are highly sensitive to congestion, packet loss and latency variation.


Two things follow for network design:


- **Capacity has to increase in large steps** . Adding sites or GPUs can quickly multiply inter-site traffic, so the network needs headroom and a fast way to add wavelengths.
- **Every bit carries a power and space cost** . Power availability has become the biggest constraint on data center growth, according to[Bloom Energy’s 2026 Data Center Power Report](https://www.powermag.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2026-power-report.pdf) . Optics that deliver more capacity per watt and per rack unit leave more of each site’s power and space for compute.


**How IPoDWDM cuts power, space and deployment time**


To add capacity quickly while using less power and space, many operators are shifting to IP over dense wavelength division multiplexing (IPoDWDM). By plugging coherent optics, such as 400G or 800G ZR and ZR+ modules, straight into router ports, IPoDWDM reduces the need for a separate transponder layer, helping cut power and space.


That shift is already gathering pace. Dell’Oro Group forecasts IPoDWDM growing at a 27% compound annual rate to more than $7 billion by 2030, while DCI revenue from IPoDWDM ZR/ZR+ optics and WDM systems grew 45% year over year in Q2 2026, as we covered in our September post,[AI is fueling IPoDWDM growth. Can your OLS keep up?](https://www.blog.adtran.com/en/ai-is-fueling-ipodwdm-growth-can-your-ols-keep-up?utm_source=technically-speaking&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=261124-why-the-trillion-dollar-data-center-expansion-depends-on-the-fiber-between-buildings) Here we focus on what that growth means for the line system.


> Compute gets the headlines. The fiber path between data centers decides whether that compute can work as one system.


**The open line system becomes the foundation**


Pluggable coherent optics still need a fiber path that can carry their wavelengths. Over distance, optical signals have to be multiplexed onto the fiber and amplified, typically every 50 to 100km depending on the fiber link. That’s the job of the open line system (OLS): the photonic layer that sits between the routers, including amplifiers, multiplexers/demultiplexers and ROADMs plus the embedded control software that keeps it running. For AI DCI, the OLS has to:


- Scale wavelength count without a redesign each time a service is added and maximize capacity per fiber pair, for example by using C- and L-bands, so operators need fewer fibers as AI traffic grows.
- Support pluggable transceivers across vendors, technologies and generations so operators can move easily from 400Gbit/s to 800Gbit/s and soon 1.6Tbit/s.
- Use AI-enhanced automation and telemetry to minimize manual work, so small teams can operate large networks.
- Keep power and footprint low, especially in edge and colocation sites where space is tight.


**What to evaluate now**


AI capacity plans are usually made in GPUs and megawatts. They should also include the optical layer. Before the next build, network teams should ask:


- How much inter-site capacity will our AI roadmap need in two to three years, and how quickly can we add it?
- Is our line system ready for 800Gbit/s pluggables and the next speed step?
- What’s our power per bit across the DCI path, and where can we reduce it?
- Can we operate many more wavelengths without adding staff at the same rate?


Compute gets the headlines. The fiber path between data centers decides whether that compute can work as one system.

**Frequently asked questions**


**What is data center interconnect (DCI)?**


Data center interconnect (DCI) is the network that links separate data center sites. It traditionally carried storage replication, backups and cloud traffic, but AI now uses it for large, sustained, delay-sensitive flows between clusters.


**What is scale-across?**


Scale-across is spreading AI training across several data centers in a metro area or region when the requirements outgrow a single facility. It depends on high-capacity, low-latency links between sites.


**What is the difference between IPoDWDM and traditional DWDM?**


Traditional DWDM uses transponders between routers and the optical line system. IPoDWDM plugs coherent optics, such as 400G or 800G ZR and ZR+ modules, directly into router ports, reducing the need for a separate transponder layer and helping cut power and space.


**How much will data centers spend in 2026?**


[Dell’Oro Group projects](https://www.delloro.com/newsroom/ai-infrastructure-buildouts-and-memory-cost-inflation-drove-data-center-capex-higher-in-1q-2026/) that worldwide data center capital spending will pass $1 trillion by the end of 2026.
